items.title: Mechanistic interpretability was a huge missed opportunity. Many people wanted to join that effort, ...
items.content: Mechanistic interpretability was a huge missed opportunity. Many people wanted to join that effort, assuming it meant a mechanistic understanding of generalization. Instead, it was a bait and switch into an extremely niche, esoteric, and largely ill-conceived effort around understanding the roles of individual neurons. This has often been a challenge in alignment and interpretability: compelling initiatives that ought to be broadly defined, or at least mean what we would expect they mean, end up being restricted to a very narrow and esoteric set of topics. For example, if someone says they work on “interpretability” it does not mean what one would naively assume, e.g., interpretable methods, algorithms, representations, or model deconstruction, understanding the data, etc., but rather sparse autoencoders, influence functions, saliency maps. What a waste!

items.content:
Deterministic tests > Written instructions

Anything that should be checked automatically should have a test case:

• Checking behavior → Unit and integration tests
• Checking formatting → Formatters and linters
• Checking types → Static type checkers
• Checking API contracts → Schema validation
• Checking edge cases → Targeted tests
• Checking regressions → Regression tests
• Checking security → Static analysis and security scans

Don't waste tokens telling an agent to follow rules you could enforce with deterministic tests.

items.title: Inspired by the spinor nature of spin–orbit-coupled electronic states, we introduce eSpinor, an SU(2...
items.content:
Inspired by the spinor nature of spin–orbit-coupled electronic states, we introduce eSpinor, an SU(2)-equivariant graph neural network that propagates spinor features to predict spin-orbit coupling (SOC)-dependent magnetic properties.

Magnetic properties such as magnetic anisotropy, excitation energies, and spin dynamics guide the design of single-molecule magnets, MRI probes, and other spin-based technologies. Predicting them often requires CASSCF-SO calculations to capture multireference electronic structure, which can take hours for a single molecular geometry.

SO(3)-equivariance has improved the accuracy of rotation-invariant energy predictions in machine-learning interatomic potentials. Can we take this idea further by imposing SU(2)-equivariance on spinor features as an inductive bias for predicting magnetic properties?

Our main contributions are:
(1) SU(2)-equivariant spinor message passing: Hamiltonian-derived spinors and classified interaction types enable gauge-covariant updates and gauge-invariant predictions
(2) Unseen-ligand generalization: Improved magnetic anisotropy and excitation-energy predictions for cobalt and dysprosium single-molecule magnet candidates
(3) Spin dynamics and solvent transfer: More accurate predictions for a dysprosium MRI probe, with benefits extending from water to methanol without retraining

Our results support SU(2)-equivariant spinor message passing as a useful inductive bias for molecular magnetism, even when the targets are integer-rank tensors or invariant scalars.

With this framework, we’re excited to help accelerate the discovery of new magnetic molecules and deepen our understanding of their spin dynamics!

items.content:
Unified multimodal models can both interpret and create images, but they usually produce a result in one pass. That limits their reliability on tasks that require several instructions to be satisfied, edits to build on one another, or visual conclusions to be checked. The article addresses whether giving these models additional computation at inference—through repeated reasoning and image refinement—can improve performance across both image generation and visual understanding.

The article introduces UniT, a framework that trains one unified model to plan, inspect its outputs, and refine them over multiple rounds. To develop it, the researchers used other models to generate and critique images, creating about 12,000 filtered examples of multi-step reasoning and editing. They fine-tuned the Bagel model on this data and tested it on image generation, compositional editing, multi-turn editing, and visual reasoning benchmarks. At inference, UniT carries out the reasoning and image work within the same model, with the number of refinement rounds serving as a controllable compute budget.

items.title: AI agents increasingly interpret images and documents from untrusted sources, yet may also access pr...
items.content:
AI agents increasingly interpret images and documents from untrusted sources, yet may also access private information and use tools that change files or systems. This creates a serious security risk: malicious instructions hidden in an image could divert an agent from the user’s request. The article tests whether such image-based prompt injection can cause harmful actions against current vision-language models, even when the user has given a clear, unrelated task and the attacker can control only the image.

The article introduces Repeat-After-Me, a black-box attack that places a short instruction on an image asking the model to start its response with a specific output. Rather than describe a malicious goal and rely on the model to interpret it, the image supplies the desired response itself—for example, a tool call—or a phrase that can prompt the model to disclose protected information. The researchers then refine the wording through repeated model queries and use a library of previously successful prompts. They tested six commercial and open-weight models across 100 document-based tasks per scenario, including private-information disclosure and exact tool calls, and also evaluated a simulated OpenClaw agent.

items.content:
To add a new book to ChapterPal, it has to be converted from its source format (PDF, LaTeX, ePUB, HTML, and plenty of other book markup formats) into ChapterPal's own Markdown flavor.

In the past, this was the hardest part, and it took me a week to convert one book.

Today, I have nearly 300 books that have already been converted, waiting in the pipeline, and, from experience, are 95% ready to be published. The remaining 5% of conversion artifacts can only be detected by looking at the book with human eyes, meaning my eyes.

And I can only physically do that for a couple of books a day; then my eyes get tired.

So, I'm the one standing between these books and the readers. I cannot clone myself, and I cannot trust the validation to an LLM because almost every issue I detect in the converted book is unique to that specific book.

What to do?

items.title: Agentic automated program repair systems can diagnose and modify code across large repositories, but...
items.content:
Agentic automated program repair systems can diagnose and modify code across large repositories, but their patches still require human review. When these systems attempt bugs they are unlikely to solve, or produce plausible-looking but incorrect fixes, developers spend time on low-value reviews and may lose trust in the technology. The article evaluates whether two screening steps can reduce this noise: deciding which bugs to attempt before repair begins, and deciding which generated patches to show for review afterward.

The authors developed and tested these two policies using an internal repair agent and three bug sets from Google’s codebase. The first policy uses a language model to estimate, from a human-written bug report, whether the repair agent is likely to succeed; bugs below a chosen threshold are skipped. The second combines build and test checks with a language-model review. In that review, one model call creates criteria for what a fix should accomplish from the bug report and original code, and another judges the proposed patch against those criteria and available test results. The evaluation included 174 human-reported bugs, 198 machine-reported null pointer errors from a live deployment, and 50 sanitizer-reported bugs. Success was assessed using reproduction tests or human correctness judgments, depending on the bug set.

items.title: Multimodal language models can answer questions about images, but their common design often treats v...
items.content:
Multimodal language models can answer questions about images, but their common design often treats visual features as if they were already compatible with language-model inputs. The article argues that this assumption is flawed: image features begin in a representation space quite different from text, and the language model itself must progressively interpret and translate them. Improving that visual processing inside the language model may therefore be as important as improving the image encoder or the connection between the two.

The article evaluates this idea through LLaViT, a modification of the widely used LLaVA architecture. It gives the language model a more active role in visual understanding in three ways: separate attention projections for image and text tokens, unrestricted two-way attention among image tokens, and image features drawn from several depths of the vision encoder to retain both fine detail and overall meaning. The team compared LLaViT with a matched LLaVA baseline across 17 benchmarks, using several language-model sizes and two image-resolution settings. Both approaches used the same image-caption pretraining data and instruction-tuning data, helping isolate the effect of the architectural changes.

Multilingual language models often answer less accurately when a question combines languages than when the same question is asked in one language. The article investigates whether this loss is linked to how a model internally represents the grammatical structure of a mixed-language question, and whether that representation can be adjusted to improve answers.

The researchers compared matched source-language, target-language, and code-switched questions across 955 factual queries, nine target languages, and a range of model families. They created controlled pairs in which the same information was expressed using either the source language’s or the target language’s grammatical frame, then compared the models’ internal representations and answer quality. They also tested CANVAS, a method that uses information from the mixed-language input itself to steer internal representations toward the source-language pattern during answering, without retraining the model.

items.title: Self-supervised image systems can learn useful patterns without labeled examples, but their internal...
items.content:
Self-supervised image systems can learn useful patterns without labeled examples, but their internal representations are difficult for people to interpret. This limits their value in scientific and other settings where teams need to understand which visual features drive a prediction, and where the relevant categories may not be known in advance. The article introduces S2COPE, a method for discovering readable visual concepts directly from unlabeled images and testing whether those concepts can support accurate and more robust image classification.

S2COPE begins with a vision-language model that proposes several descriptions for each image. A separate image-and-text model scores how well each description matches its image and distinguishes it from other images. The system uses these scores to prefer more informative descriptions and repeatedly fine-tunes the proposal model. The concept discovery process uses no image labels, class names, concept annotations, or human judgments. The researchers trained the model on unlabeled natural-history images and tested its concepts, without further adaptation, on eight datasets covering nature, faces, medical images, and physics.

items.title: Online platforms often recommend options using feedback from people who have tried them. When users ...
items.content:
Online platforms often recommend options using feedback from people who have tried them. When users make choices mainly for their own immediate benefit, they may avoid testing uncertain options, leaving the platform with incomplete evidence and causing a weaker option to remain popular. The article asks whether this problem disappears when each person can make several choices in a short episode and has some incentive to explore for their own future benefit.

The article analyzes a stylized Bayesian bandit model. Two options have unknown, fixed success rates, and each new agent sees the history of prior choices and outcomes before making several consecutive decisions. Agents choose the strategy that maximizes their own expected episode utility, which may depend on the sum, maximum, minimum, or another qualifying function of the episode’s rewards. A skip option and small selection costs represent the effort involved in trying an option. The analysis establishes theoretical results under a shared Beta prior and binary outcomes; it also examines some extensions to more options and to settings with no selection costs.
